content: AD-36 is one of the 51 known types of adenoviruses that can infect humans. It was first identified as being associated with obesity in chickens by Dr. Nikhil Dhurandhar. A positive correlation has been observed between the presence of AD-36 antibodies in the blood and increased body fat. Previous studies have demonstrated that chickens or mice injected with similar types of viruses exhibit statistically significant weight gain. In some cases, a fivefold increase in fat storage was observed among the test subjects. The weight gain associated with AD-36 infection has a distinctive signature. While antibodies to the virus can now be detected, the weight gain is unusual in that levels of lipids, triglycerides, and cholesterol in the blood are markedly low or even absent. This is in contrast to typical obesity, where these substances are usually found in abundance in the bloodstream as part of the natural metabolic processes. The current hypothesis is that these chemicals are being stored within cells rather than being excreted into the bloodstream, although their exact fate remains unknown. Experimental findings have shown that AD-36 increases adiposity in chickens and other non-human subjects. However, it is important to note that AD-36 is not the sole or even a primary cause of obesity. While it has been shown to increase fat accumulation, the duration of this effect is not well understood, and it does not appear to persist for many years. Recent studies have also examined other human adenoviruses, including AD-37 and AD-2. AD-37 demonstrated a similar correlation with increased fat tissue, as it induced human stem cells to differentiate into fat cells. However, unlike AD-36, AD-37 was found to increase cholesterol levels. In contrast, AD-2 was observed to reduce body fat in test subjects. The most significant takeaway from these experiments, conducted in 2004 for AD-36 and in 2007 for AD-37, is that the effects of adenoviruses on body fat are variable and complex. It is crucial to understand that adenoviruses are not the sole cause of obesity. Further research is necessary to determine whether these viruses contribute to long-term obesity and to elucidate the mechanisms underlying their effects.
